title: How does object-oriented design affect testability?
description: Why untestable code is usually a design problem, the seams that make units testable, and how DI, immutability, and small interfaces map to fast reliable tests.

data.text: **Question:** How does object-oriented design affect testability?

Testability is a design property, not a testing tool feature. A unit is easy to test when you can **construct it with all its dependencies, run one behavior, and assert on observable results — with no database, network, clock, or global state involved**. That requires constructor injection of small interfaces, no hidden static dependencies, and logic that returns values instead of reaching out to the world. If a class can only be exercised by spinning up SQL Server and a mail server, the class's design — not the test suite — is the problem.

**The design moves that create testability:**
- **Constructor injection**: dependencies arrive as parameters, so a test supplies fakes. New'ing `new SqlDatabase()` or a static call inside a method is an untestable seam
- **Small, behavior-shaped interfaces**: `IClock.UtcNow` and `IEmailSender.SendAsync` are trivially fakeable; a 20-method `IDataContext` is not
- **Pure core logic**: methods that compute a value from inputs (pricing, validation, state transitions) are the easiest and most valuable to test. Push I/O to the edges
- **No temporal coupling**: if testing requires calling `Init()` then `Login()` then `Work()`, tests encode fragile sequences. Design so any valid state is constructible directly
- **Determinism**: hidden reliance on `DateTime.Now`, `Guid.NewGuid()`, randomness, or thread scheduling makes tests flaky — inject them

**The payoff beyond tests:** the same seams that enable unit tests enable swapping implementations in production (different queue, cache, or AI provider per environment) — testability and flexibility are the same property viewed from two angles.

**When your code is hard to test, refactor the code:** extract the tangled logic into a pure function/class that takes its dependencies as parameters, then unit-test that. Keep a thin integration-test layer for the I/O edges you deliberately didn't fake.

data.title: Untestable vs testable order discount logic
Don't fake everything
data.text: Faking the thing under test's own logic (e.g., mocking EF Core's query pipeline to 'test' your repository) produces tests that pass while production breaks. Fake *your* boundaries (clock, queue, third-party API); use real in-memory/containers for infrastructure you're configuring. The best test doubles are for dependencies you don't own.

Interviewers want to hear:
- That hard-to-test code is a design smell (hidden dependencies, side-effect mixing)
- Constructor DI as the mechanism, not a framework ritual
- Pushing I/O to edges and keeping a pure core
- A concrete refactor story: extracted a class, injected a clock, and the flaky test became deterministic

items: Mocking every collaborator so tests only verify your mocks
Making interfaces public just so tests can see internals — prefer testing through behavior
Static helper classes and singletons that force global state into unit tests
Sleeping in tests to wait for async work instead of exposing completion
Claiming 'it's hard to test because the framework makes it hard' — usually it's the design

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Testability = construct, run, assert — with I/O and time injected, not baked in
Constructor DI + small interfaces + pure core logic are the design levers
Hard-to-test code is usually badly coupled code; refactor the production code
Fake your boundaries, use real infrastructure for the rest
data.takeaway: If a class can't be tested without a database and a calendar, the class — not the test — needs a redesign.
